prompt: Where does a language model's parametric knowledge live?
hint: The name says it.

choices.text: In the system prompt sent with every request
choices.why: The system prompt is text in the window: in-context knowledge, gone when the request ends.

choices.text: In its weights, fixed when training stopped
choices.why: Right. That is why nothing a user does afterwards adds to it.

choices.text: In a search index the model consults before answering
choices.why: There is no index inside a model. It consults nothing; it produces likely text.

choices.text: In the conversation history the provider keeps for each user
choices.why: Whatever a provider stores, the model reads only what each request sends; that is in-context, not parametric.

prompt: Of the three ways a company's fact can be missing from a model, why is the changed fact the hardest to catch?
hint: Think about what is behind the answer.

choices.text: Changed facts are rarer than private ones
choices.why: How common it is does not make it harder to catch; how convincing the answer is does.

choices.text: Training removes facts once they change
choices.why: Training never hears about the change. The old fact stays in the weights.

choices.text: The model refuses to answer whenever a fact it learnt has since changed
choices.why: It does the opposite: it answers with the old fact, confidently.

choices.text: It was right once, so it is stated as well as any true fact
choices.why: Yes. The model learnt it well; nothing in the text marks it as out of date.

prompt: Asked how many days it gives to return a printed book, llama3.2:3b answered with a library's loan rules. Which behaviour is that?
hint: Nothing but the question was in the request.

choices.text: Reading a help-centre article about libraries
choices.why: Nothing was in the request but the question. There was nothing to read.

choices.text: Answering the nearest question it knows, in the form of an answer
choices.why: Right: no knowledge of Marginalia, and still a fluent, confident reply about something else.

choices.text: Mixing up two documents that had both been sent in its prompt together
choices.why: Its prompt held no documents at all.

choices.text: Refusing a question it was not trained on
choices.why: It refused the phone question, not this one, and that is the danger: nothing in the text says which kind of reply it is.

prompt: Knowledge carried in the weights is called parametric; knowledge carried in the request is called ___ knowledge.
hint: Where in the request does it sit?

prompt: What does `OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1` in `env.sh` do?
hint: The SDK is OpenAI's; the server is not.

choices.text: Sends OpenAI's SDK to Ollama on your own machine instead of OpenAI's servers
choices.why: Right. Ollama speaks the same wire format, so the SDK talks to it unchanged.

choices.text: Downloads llama3.2:3b the first time a program runs
choices.why: `ollama pull` downloads models; the variable only says where requests go.

choices.text: Gives the programs a free OpenAI account
choices.why: No request leaves the machine, and no account is involved anywhere.

choices.text: Tells PostgreSQL where to find the vectors
choices.why: `PGDATABASE` is the database's; this one is the model's.

prompt: Why do the course's programs ask the model for `temperature=0`?
hint: What would a rerun print without it?

choices.text: It makes the model more accurate
choices.why: It removes randomness from the choice of words; it does not add knowledge.

choices.text: Reruns on one machine then print the same reply, nearly every time
choices.why: Right. Nearly, not always: reused work can change a word, and another machine or model changes more.

choices.text: Ollama refuses requests without it
choices.why: Ollama has a default; the programs set it so that a rerun is repeatable.

choices.text: It makes every student's reply identical to the lesson's
choices.why: A different processor or version of Ollama still changes the words, which is why the lessons read patterns, not wording.

prompt: By the `grep` after `docs.sh`, how many times does "14 days" appear across the corpus?
hint: Add the four counts.

prompt: What changed in the model between ask.py and with_doc.py?
hint: Compare the two requests, not the two models.

choices.text: It remembered the policy from an earlier question
choices.why: Nothing carries over between requests; without the policy it would talk about libraries again.

choices.text: It switched to a larger context window
choices.why: Ollama served it with 4,096 tokens both times; 1,166 fit easily.

choices.text: Nothing; the request carried the policy
choices.why: Right. The knowledge lives in the request, for the length of the request.

choices.text: Its weights were updated with the returns policy
choices.why: Nothing updates weights during a request.

prompt: with_doc.py's reply gave thirty days and no `[1]`, although the policy was numbered. Why?
hint: Read the system message again.

choices.text: The number was cut off by the context window
choices.why: The request was 1,166 tokens, well inside 4,096.

choices.text: Nothing in the request asked it to cite
choices.why: Right. A number makes a citation possible; an instruction asks for it, and lesson 7 checks it.

choices.text: llama3.2:3b cannot cite sources
choices.why: It cited [1] in tiny_rag.py, where the system message asked.

choices.text: The answer came from its training, not the policy
choices.why: Without the policy it answered about libraries. Thirty days came from the source.

prompt: How many prompt tokens did with_doc.py's request carry for the return-window question?
hint: The program prints it after the reply.

prompt: A colleague puts the 2025 returns policy in the prompt by mistake. What happens to the answer about return postage?
hint: The model can only be as current as its text.

choices.text: The model notices the date and refuses to use it
choices.why: Nothing tells it which year is current unless the prompt says so; lesson 7 is about that.

choices.text: It gets the 2025 answer, quoted faithfully and cited
choices.why: Yes. The document is the authority; a wrong document gives a wrong answer that looks checked.

choices.text: The model blends 2025 with what it learnt in training
choices.why: With a source present, a model mostly answers from the source. One that also blended in its training would be worse, not better.

choices.text: The citation number exposes the mistake to the customer
choices.why: A citation to [1] says nothing about whether [1] is current.

prompt: By count.py, how many tokens do the thirteen documents add up to?
hint: The last line.

prompt: everything.py sent about 9,000 tokens and the reply reported `prompt tokens: 2050`. What happened?
hint: Ollama's log said `truncating input prompt`.

choices.text: Ollama cut the prompt to fit the window and kept its end
choices.why: Right. The question survived; the documents at the start, the delivery prices among them, did not.

choices.text: The provider refused the request
choices.why: Nothing refused. A reply came back, which is what makes this failure easy to miss.

choices.text: The model read everything and summarised it in 2,050 tokens
choices.why: prompt_tokens counts what it read, not what it wrote.

choices.text: tiktoken and llama count tokens four times differently
choices.why: They differ by a few percent, not by a factor of four.

prompt: A provider launches a model with a ten-million-token window. Which cost of sending the whole corpus with every question does it remove?
hint: A bigger window moves the limit.

choices.text: None of the three; it only removes the refusal
choices.why: Right. The request now fits, and every other cost remains and grows with the corpus.

choices.text: The chance that unrelated text pulls the reply off course
choices.why: More unrelated text means more chances to use the wrong part.

choices.text: The price of every question paying for every document
choices.why: Every token is still billed, whatever the window.

choices.text: The time spent reading the whole prompt before replying
choices.why: The model still reads it all first; a longer prompt is slower to read.

prompt: At the lesson's illustrative 3 per million input tokens, what do ten thousand prompts carrying the 8,914 tokens of the documents cost? Round to a whole number.
In the diagram, which half runs every time somebody asks?
hint: The other half runs when documents change.

choices.text: Rebuilding the index with the new question in it
choices.why: Questions are not added to the index; it holds documents.

choices.text: Fine-tuning the generator on the retrieved chunks
choices.why: No training happens at query time; the chunks only go into the prompt.

choices.text: Cutting every document into chunks and embedding each chunk once more
choices.why: That is indexing, which runs before anybody asks.

choices.text: Embedding the question, searching, and writing from what was found
choices.why: Right: the query half.

prompt: Put the query half in order, from the question to the answer.
hint: The search needs the question as a vector.
items: Embed the question with the same model as the chunks
Find the nearest chunks in the index
Put them in a prompt, numbered, with the question
The generator writes an answer that cites the numbers

prompt: For the return-window question, tiny_rag.py also retrieved the replaced 2025 policy, second at 0.807, and the reply was right. What does that say?
hint: What told the model which source was current?

choices.text: Retrieval failed, because it returned an old document
choices.why: It returned what was most similar, which is its job; nothing told it the document was old.

choices.text: The reply was right by luck: nothing told the model which source is current
choices.why: Right. For return postage the old policy came first and the reply quoted it.

choices.text: llama3.2:3b knows the 2025 policy was replaced
choices.why: It has never seen either policy outside the prompt.

choices.text: Both halves are now proven to work
choices.why: One right answer proves nothing about the next; lesson 8 measures thirty.

prompt: How many `## ` sections did grep count in the corpus?
hint: The number tiny_rag.py chose from.

prompt: Why did the 2025 section on return postage beat the current policy for "Who pays for the return postage?"
hint: Compare what each section is about.

choices.text: The current policy was missing from the index when tiny_rag.py searched it
choices.why: It was there and came second, at 0.530.

choices.text: Newer documents are penalised by the embedding model
choices.why: The model has no idea of dates; it embeds text.

choices.text: That section is all about postage; today's rule is one sentence of many
choices.why: Right: 0.798 against 0.530. Similarity measures topic, not truth or date.

choices.text: tiny_rag.py sorts by file name
choices.why: It sorts by score; the scores are printed.

prompt: Match each run from this lesson to the failure it showed.
hint: One failure was not seen in any run.

pairs.left: Who pays for the return postage?
pairs.right: A replaced document was found and quoted
The right section found and the price cited

pairs.left: How many days do I have to return a printed book?
pairs.right: Two sources that disagree, both retrieved

pairs.left: Can I place an order by phone?
pairs.right: Nothing answered, and a rule was invented

right_distractors: The answer was retrieved and the reply missed it

prompt: Which question should go to a database query instead of a retrieval pipeline?
hint: A retrieval system reads a few passages.

choices.text: What does error E-4102 mean in the affiliate API?
choices.why: The API reference's error table answers it.

choices.text: How long is a gift card valid?
choices.why: One passage answers it: two years.

choices.text: How many orders were refunded last month?
choices.why: Right: a count over records, written in no document.

choices.text: Can I return a signed copy?
choices.why: One section of the returns policy answers it.

prompt: A support bot answers from memory that Marginalia's phone line opens at 9 am. What would retrieval change, given today's documents?
hint: Is a phone line in any document?

choices.text: Nothing, because retrieval only helps with recent facts
choices.why: It helps with private and changed facts too, and with saying what is not covered.

choices.text: The bot would find the phone number and correct the hours
choices.why: There is no phone number to find; no document mentions one.

choices.text: With the documents in the prompt, it could say they do not cover it
choices.why: Right: that is what with_doc.py printed for the same question. Lesson 7 makes it a rule rather than a habit.

choices.text: The bot would quote the 2025 policy
choices.why: The 2025 policy says nothing about phones either.

prompt: Retrieval-augmented generation: a ___ runs first, and the model writes from its results.
hint: What finds the passages?

prompt: Which of these does retrieval-augmented generation fix? Choose all that apply.
hint: Retrieval cures one disease: the model not having the text.

choices.text: An index that still holds the replaced 2025 policy
choices.why: No: retrieval found it and quoted it. Fixing that is a matter of what you store and filter.

choices.text: A question about a total across every order
choices.why: No: that needs a query over records, not a few passages.

choices.text: A model that misreads tables
choices.why: No: it misreads them in the prompt as anywhere else.

choices.text: A model that never saw the private support handbook
choices.why: Yes: the handbook can be retrieved and put in the prompt.

choices.text: A model trained before this year's policy existed
choices.why: Yes: the new policy is retrieved at query time.
